about: THE WINTER (Design/research_indie_and_concept.md 4.4: 'winter is the reckoning'; Design/research_scale_to_fleets.md 5: 'the winter council'). Four parts. reckoning: how the screen runs and its lines for a good, a middling and a bad year. cards: forty things that can happen over a winter ashore, in the engine's own card format (exactly the fields of encounters/harbour_793.json, so the loader would take them); their conditions and effects use only the variables of Cond.cs and the verbs of Effects.cs, checked by a script that mirrors the loader. writing: the words for every key the cards use, the line shown after each choice, and one line of what each card's picture shows (writing-file format: lift it into Data/writing/winter.json when the cards go live). inheritance: what an heir keeps, pays and loses. remembered: twelve ways a life is written in the chronicle, from a beggar to the king's friend. (?) marks what was not checked against a source tonight. Sums of silver are starting guesses on the scale of Design/content/CHAINS.md. A draft in the game's own file, for the user to overwrite. Written 4 Oct 2026.

reckoning.about: THE WINTER RECKONING (research_indie_and_concept.md 4.4; research_scale_to_fleets.md 5, the winter council). Once a year, the clock held: the year's log is read back, the debt is met or not, the boat is hauled, men leave and come, the heir grows a year, and one thing is chosen to build. The lines below are what the screen says about the year as a whole, before the log's own entries. {year}, {gain}, {loss}, {name}, {port}, {lost} and {feast} are filled in.
how_it_runs: 1. It opens when she is laid up after Michaelmas (29 September) at a port where the house has a plot, a host or its home, and at the latest at Martinmas (11 November). The screen sets 'flag wintering for <days till Easter>': every winter card asks for it.
2. The year is judged good, middling or bad (the rules under 'years') and one of that kind's lines is shown, then the voyage log's own entries in order: the short saga of the year.
3. The debt: the card harbour.winter.count_debt while any is owed.
4. The two cards of every winter: harbour.winter.crew_keep and harbour.winter.haul_and_tar.

5. Then two more cards (three in a year with a death, a wreck or a birth), drawn by weight from those whose 'when' holds in the winter's months, scheduled cards first, none twice. Cards whose note says 'without a draw' are played in the chronicle's own years.
6. The one thing built over the winter: a choice from 'one_thing'.
7. The chronicle's news of the year, as it has reached this port.
8. Easter: the flag lapses, the men are on the bank, and spring begins with three things known: the debt's new day, the fairs' dates, the first rumour.

good.when: The year's gain after wages, bread, tolls and gifts is 240 d or more (half the first debt), no boat was lost and no man died.
lines: This year the house did well. {gain} pennies came home over what went out, and no man was lost.
This year the boat came home deep, and the debt grew smaller.
A good year. The wine sold where it was wanted, and the news reached you before it reached the others.
This year there was peace on the water, and the house grew by {gain} pennies.
The men have new shoes and the chest is heavier than it was at Easter. Nothing else need be said.
This year {name} was spoken of at {port} as a man who comes back.

middling.when: The year's gain is between a loss of 60 d and a gain of 240 d, and the boat is whole.
lines: This year the house neither grew nor shrank. The boat is whole and the men are fed.
A year like most. Some legs made silver and some made stories.
This year {gain} pennies came home. It is enough for the winter and not enough for the count.
The boat came home. That is the first thing, and this year it is nearly the only one.
This year nothing is written of the house, which is a kind of luck.
Bread till Easter and tar for the seams. The rest waits for another year.

bad.when: The year's loss is more than 60 d, or a boat was lost, or two men died, or the debt's day passed unpaid.
lines: This year the house went backward by {loss} pennies.
A bad year. The price fell before the boat arrived, and it did so twice.
This year the sea took {lost} and gave nothing back.
This year there was a great hunger in the chest.
The men were paid before the count was. Let it be remembered that it was done so.
This year the boat came home light, and one bench is empty.

paid: This year the debt was paid, on the day, in good pennies. The count's man broke his half of the stick and gave you the pieces.
This year {name} owed no man anything.
part: Part of the debt was paid at Martinmas and part was not. The stick has fewer notches and the count has a longer memory.
The count took what there was and named another day.
unpaid: The debt's day came and went. The count's man came with it and did not go.
This year the count had a claim on the boat, and said so before witnesses.

reckoning.voice: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's: one fact to a sentence, the year first, no reasons given. Model: the Chronicle for 793 (texts_793.json chronicle_793, Giles 1847). These lines are the game's own, written in that manner; none is quoted.

Drinking to the old gods at midwinter is described only in later Norse books; the Church's list of forbidden customs is the Indiculus superstitionum (c. 743). In the first merchant's years one of the two is Ravn, the house's own man of the old faith (riddles_793.json r-gest-01).

writing.about: The words of the winter cards, in the format of a writing file: title, intention and label keys repeat the plain words on the cards; '.after' keys are the outcome of each choice as a fact; 'art.' keys say what the card's picture shows.

entries.text: A child is coming
Your wife's time has come in the dark of the year. The wise woman of the bank can be sent for. The priest says prayer is enough, and that the woman knows charms.
A lamp-lit room in a timber house at night: a woman in a headcloth carrying a bowl of steaming water past a man who stands useless by the door; snow in the doorway behind him.
Send for the wise woman
A child is born alive and the mother lives. The wise woman takes her six pennies and a loaf, and says the child will sail.
The child does not live the night. The mother mends slowly. The wise woman will not take the pennies.
Let the women of the house manage
The women of the house do what women have always done. A child is born alive.
It goes badly. The child is buried before it is named, and nobody says whose fault that was.
Send for her, and promise wax to the church if both live
Both live. You pay the wise woman her six pennies and the church its wax, and count it cheap.
The child does not live the night. No wax is owed. You give it anyway, later, and say nothing about why.
The font
The child must be baptised within the month, and someone must lift it from the water. Whoever does is kin to you from that day, and to the child.
Inside a small timber church: a priest in a plain alb holding a baby over a stone basin, three men waiting behind him with their caps in their hands; grey winter light from one window.
Ask the count's man
The count's man lifts the child from the water and gives it a silver penny. He will know your name when the debt is spoken of.
Ask a merchant of the bank
A neighbour with a boat of his own stands sponsor. His house and yours share bread at feasts now, and he asks what you paid for wine at Colonia.
Ask your own steersman
Your steersman holds the child as if it were a full bailer. The crew drink to it. It costs you nothing and binds a good man.
The child burns
The child has had a fever three nights now and it will not break. The leech is across the river. The wise woman is next door. The church is always open.
A cradle by a hearth in the dark, a man kneeling with his hand on a child's forehead, a woman behind him holding a bunch of dried herbs.
Fetch the leech across the river
The leech lets no blood from one so small. He gives betony in warm ale and sits up. On the fourth morning the fever is gone.
The fever breaks at last, but the child is slow to mend and thin all year.
Ask the wise woman for her herbs
She binds a root to the child's wrist and gives it something bitter. It sleeps. The priest hears of the root and says nothing, this time.
The root does nothing that anyone can see. The fever breaks in its own time, and the child is thin all year.
Carry the child to the church and keep watch there
You keep the night by the altar with the child inside your cloak. At dawn it asks for milk.
You keep three nights by the altar. The child lives, and is thin all year.
A wife for the house
Your mother says a house with a boat and no wife is a boat with no keel. There is a neighbour's daughter who can keep a tally. There is also the daughter of the Englishman you deal with over the sea.
A church door in thin winter sun: a man and a young woman with their right hands joined, a priest between them, an old woman counting pennies into another old woman's palm.
Marry the neighbour's daughter
The bride-gift is paid before witnesses, and the morning-gift after the first night: a cow and the loom. The priest blesses it at the church door. The bank eats at your cost for two days.
Send word across the sea to the Englishman
Her father agrees by the last ship. She comes at Easter with a chest, a loom weight from home and her own speech. Your children will have two tongues and two harbours.
Not this year
The house stays as it is. Your mother says nothing, several times a day.
An offer for your sister

The house that undercut you on wine all summer sends an old woman with a proposal: their eldest son for your sister. It would end the quarrel. Your sister has seen him and has not said what she thinks.
An old woman in a dark cloak sitting very upright on a bench by the hearth, a young woman at the loom behind her with her back turned, listening.
Agree, and pay her portion
It is done before Lent. The two houses sit at one table at the wedding and are careful with each other. He does not undercut you again.
Ask her first
She says he has good hands and a fool for a father, and that she can manage both. Her portion is eighty pennies.
She says no, and why, at some length. You carry a shorter answer back. The other house is cool, and your own thinks better of you.
Refuse
You send the old woman home with a cheese and a no. They take it badly and politely.
A Dane's offer

A Dane you have traded beside for two summers says that where he comes from, friends bring up each other's sons. He will take a boy of yours north, or leave his own with you. He means it as an honour.
Two men on a bench by a fire, one fair and broad in a Danish cloak with a ring pin, a small boy asleep against his knee; the other man looking at the boy.
Send your boy north with him
The boy goes aboard the Dane's ship at Easter with a new knife and does not look back. He will come home in four years talking like a Dane and rowing like one.
Take his son into your house
A Danish boy of nine sits at your table and eats like a man of thirty. By midwinter the whole house is swearing in his tongue.
Thank him and decline
He shrugs. Among his own people it would be an insult. He knows you are a Frisian, and lets it pass.
Letters for the boy
The schoolmaster at the bishop's church takes boys for the winter: the psalms, the letters, reckoning on the fingers. He says your son is quick. He also says he would make a monk.
A cold stone room with a bench of small boys holding wax tablets, a thin master in a black habit pointing with a rod at letters scratched on a board.
Send him for the winter
By Easter the boy can read the toll man's tally and the first psalm, and has opinions about your accounts.
Give him to the church for good
His hand is wrapped in the altar cloth with your gift. He is the church's now. You have a son who will write, and no son to sail.
Keep him at the oar
He learns to scull, to splice and to keep quiet when the toll man talks. There are worse schools.
Twelve winters
Your eldest is twelve: old enough to swear his oath to the king with the other free men, and to pull an oar. He has asked every day since Martinmas.
A boy of twelve standing on a river bank in winter beside a hauled-up boat, one hand flat on her planking, looking at the water.
Take him aboard at Easter
He has the bow oar and the bailer. The men are easier on him than you are.
Leave him ashore to learn the house
He keeps the store and the tally with his mother. He will know prices before he knows the sea.
One more winter
He says nothing. He mends nets on the bank, where he can see the boats go out.
A death in the house
Your father's brother, who taught you the river, dies at Candlemas after a week in bed. He was baptised as a grown man and kept some of the old ways. The priest waits to hear what you want.
A small churchyard under snow, an open grave with four men lowering a shrouded body on ropes, a priest reading, a row of old men standing apart with their hoods up.
A grave by the church wall, and masses
The soul's gift is paid at the open grave. A mass is sung on the thirtieth day. He lies with his head to the west and nothing in his hands.
A plain grave in the churchyard
He is buried among the poor of the bank, decently. The priest says the short office.
The churchyard, with his knife and a coin beside him
You put his knife at his belt and a penny in his fist when the priest's back is turned. The old men of the bank nod.
The priest sees the knife and takes it out again in front of everyone. He says the law is plain about the customs of the heathen, and so is he.
You lie sick
From Candlemas to the middle of Lent you cannot stand. The house walks softly. There is a boat, a debt, a chest and a plot, and nothing has been said before witnesses about any of them.
A box bed with a sick man propped on a bolster, six men standing round it with their caps off, a woman at the foot holding a child.
Call six neighbours and name your heir
Six free men of the bank stand round the bed and hear it said: who has the boat, who has the house, what the widow keeps. Whatever comes, there will be no lawsuit.
Send a gift to the church for your soul
The priest brings the oil and takes the silver. You are better by Easter. He does not offer to give it back.
Lie still and say nothing
It passes, as most things do.
It passes slowly. You go aboard at Easter with a cough and a stick.
The men at Martinmas
The boat is on the bank and the season's shares are paid. Your men look at you. Bread and ale till Easter, or each his own road till the water opens?
Four men sitting on an upturned boat on a frosty bank with their sea-bags at their feet, all looking the same way, at the viewer.
Keep them on bread and ale till Easter
They sleep in the boat shed, mend gear, and eat more than you thought four men could. At Easter they are all there.
Keep them for their work on the boat
They scrape, tar and re-rivet for their keep. The boat is sound by Candlemas and the men are sick of tar.
Let them go till Easter
They go to their own hearths. At Easter all of them are on the bank, thinner.
At Easter one does not come. He has taken a place on a bigger ship, and sends his regards.
A man of yours marries
Your lookout is marrying a fisherman's daughter after Epiphany. Her father would like a son-in-law who stays ashore. The man himself has not decided.
A long table in a fisherman's house, a young man and a girl at its head looking stunned, an older man in a merchant's cloak filling the father's cup.
Stand him the bride-ale
You pay for the ale and sit at the bride's father's right hand. By the end of the night he has agreed that a share of a good boat is better than a net.
Offer him a share instead of a wage
He will sail for a part of what the boat makes. He stays. So does his new father-in-law's interest in your accounts.
Wish him well
He marries, and is on the bank at Easter all the same.
He marries, and takes up the net. You need a lookout.
A tooth at the ale-wife's
One of your men has knocked out a Frank's tooth at the ale-wife's, over a remark about Frisian cloaks. The law of the Frisians has a price for every wound, and the lawman knows it by heart.
An ale-house interior: a big man holding his jaw, a smaller one being held back by two friends, an ale-wife with her arms folded in front of the cask.
Pay the wound-price
The lawman names the price for a front tooth, which is more than for a back one. You pay. Your man says the remark was worth it.
Swear with oath-helpers that the Frank struck first
Five neighbours swear with you. The Frank pays for the ale and keeps his opinion of cloaks to himself.
The ale-wife swears the other way, and she was sober. You pay the price and half again.
Make him ask pardon before the whole ale-house
He stands bareheaded and says the words. The Frank accepts, with a gap in his smile. Your man does not speak to you for a week.
The oldest hand
Your oldest hand dies in his bed at midwinter, which he always said he would not. A share of the last voyage was still owed him. His widow has not asked.
A small dark house, an old woman sitting by a cold hearth with a sea-chest open beside her, a man in the doorway holding a leather purse.
Pay her his share and something over
You carry it to her yourself. The crew hear of it before you are home.
Pay her what was owed, to the penny
It is counted out on her table before a witness. Nobody can say more or less.
Say the voyage made a loss
Nobody can prove otherwise. The men you try to hire at Easter have heard the story.
A boy at the door
A neighbour's boy of fourteen asks for a place at the oar. He is strong and has never been past the river mouth. His mother came an hour before him and asked you to say no.
A big-boned boy of fourteen standing in a doorway with snow on his shoulders, twisting his cap; behind him, across the yard, a woman watching from another door.
Take him
He is on the bank before dawn every day for a week in case you sail early. His mother sends bread for him and none for you.
Take him, and promise her he stays in the river this year
She makes you say it twice. If you take him over the bar before next winter she will know, and so will the whole bank.
Tell him to come back in two winters
He goes away without a word. You will see him at the oar of another man's boat by midsummer.
Midwinter

The twelve days are coming. The Christians of the bank keep them with mass and meat. Two of your men who keep the old ways would pour ale to the old powers for a good year, as their fathers did, and they ask if they may do it under your roof.
A crowded room lit by a long fire, a boar's head on a board, men with horns and cups; at the open door two men are slipping out into the dark with a small cask.
Keep the feast: ale and meat for the crew and the neighbours
For twelve days nobody works. The priest eats at your table on the third and praises the pork.
Keep the feast, and let the two pour their ale as well
They pour to a good year and peace, quietly, down by the boat. Then they come in and eat with everyone else. Nobody tells the priest.
Somebody tells the priest. He preaches on it at Epiphany without naming you, and looks at you while he does it.
Keep it small this year
Mass, a hen, and an early night. The men remember other winters.
The boat on the bank
She is hauled above the flood line on rollers. The seams want tar, three strakes weep at the lands, and the rivets by the stem are loose. The wright has looked and named his price.
A clinker boat on rollers on a frozen bank, her mast lying beside her, a man with a tar pot and a brush under her quarter, smoke from a fire of shavings.
Pay the wright
He drives new rivets, lays tarred wool in the seams and burns his mark by the stem. She will be dry at Easter.
Do it with your own men
Tar to the elbows for a week. She is tight.
She looks tight. In the first chop of spring you learn which rivet was not.
Leave her till spring
She will float. She will also let the sea in when it matters most.
The wright's offer
The wright walks round her twice. The keel is good for twenty years, he says. For silver he will scarf in a new stem and add a strake each side: she would carry a fifth more and ship less water.
A boat on the bank with her top strake off, a wright sighting along a new plank held up by two boys, oak chips on the snow.
Add the strake
He works till Lent. She sits the same in the water and holds four casks more. She rows heavier, and the men say so.
The new stem only
A new stem of grown oak, scarfed and riveted. The old one goes on the fire and burns for two days.
She will do as she is
The wright shrugs. He has seen boats older than her come home, and newer ones not.
Fire in the row
Shouting in the night. The thatch three houses up the row is alight and the wind is toward you. There is time to do one thing well.
A row of thatched houses at night, the far ones blazing, sparks blowing along the roofs; in front a man dragging a chest across the road, people running with buckets.
Carry out the chest and the scales
The chest, the scales and the tally sticks stand in the road. The house burns to the sills behind them. Walls can be built again by Easter.
The roof comes down before the second trip. The chest is out. A bag of silver under the floor is a lump among the ashes.
Pull down the house between, with hooks
Ten men and two boat-hooks bring the neighbour's roof down into the road before the fire reaches it. Your house stands. His does not, and he thanks you, in time.
The gap is not wide enough. Both houses go.
Get the neighbours' children out first
Four children and a grandmother are carried out through the back. Your own house burns with everything in it but the chest. The bank does not forget who did what that night.
The sea comes in
A north-west gale on a spring tide. By midnight the water is over the bank and in the lower houses, and still rising. The boat is on her rollers. The church stands on the only high ground.
Black water up to the eaves of low houses under a torn sky, a small boat with four men rowing between the roofs, people clinging to a thatch; on a mound behind, a wooden church with a light in it.
Carry the stock up to the church mound
Casks, bales and the chest go up the mound on men's backs in the dark. By morning the house is knee-deep and everything you own is dry in the church porch.
Launch the boat for the people on the roofs
You take eleven people off roofs and out of trees before dawn. The stock in the house is spoiled. Nobody on this bank will let you pay for ale again.
You take eleven people off the roofs. A floating beam stoves a plank on the way back. The stock is spoiled as well.
Stay on your own roof and wait
The water goes down with the tide, as it always has. It takes the malt, the salt and the lowest course of the wall with it.
The river stands
The river has stood for three weeks. Carts cross on the ice. Where a hull was left afloat, the ice works at it day and night.
A frozen river under a white sky, a loaded cart and oxen crossing it, a boat fast in the ice near the bank with two men swinging axes round her.
Haul her higher, with hired oxen
Six oxen and a morning. She sits in the lee of the shed with her mast down, and the ice can do what it likes.
Cut her free each morning
Every dawn, axes. The men hate it. The hull is whole when the thaw comes.
One night is colder than the axes are early. The ice lifts a plank from the lands.
Load a sledge and sell across the ice
Wine and salt go to the farms across the water on runners. They pay well for not having to walk.
The ice sings under the load halfway over. You lighten the sledge by a cask and come home.
A man in the storehouse
Your men catch a man in the storehouse at night with a sack of your malt. He is from the hungry end of the bank and has four children. By the law he is yours to bring before the count.
A storehouse by lantern light: two boatmen holding a thin man by the arms, a spilled sack of grain at his feet, the merchant in his shirt holding the lantern up to see his face.
Take him to the count's court
The court awards you twice the malt's worth and takes its own fine besides. He can pay neither. He works it off as the count's man, and not a free one.
Take the malt back, and his knife as a pledge
He goes home without his knife. It hangs on your wall till he brings a day's work for it, which he does, at Easter.
Give him the sack
He does not thank you. He cannot look at you. In spring his wife leaves a basket of eels at your door and is gone before it is opened.
The loom by the door
The loom stands where the light is. With wool enough, the women of the house can have cloaks ready by Easter: the Frisian kind that the Franks pay for and complain about.
An upright loom by an open door with low sun coming through the warp, two women passing the weft, loom weights of baked clay hanging in a row.
Buy wool for the loom
Three cloaks lie folded in the chest by Easter. They are the full length. Tell the Franks.
Have them weave for the sail instead
Three bolts of tight sailcloth, greased and rolled. The women say a cloak is more thanks for less work.
Let them weave for the house only
Everyone in the house has a whole shirt by Candlemas. Nothing goes in the chest.
A claim on your landing

A man from across the river swears that the landing where your boat lies was his father's, and that yours took it. The court sits after Epiphany. The lawman says there are three ways: your oath with helpers, the lots on the altar, or a bargain.
A church interior: an altar with two small bundles of white wool on it, a boy of seven reaching for one, two rows of grim men watching from either side.
Find eleven men to swear with you
Eleven free men lay their hands with yours on the relics and say your oath is clean. The claim falls. You owe eleven men a dinner.
Nine come. Two have remembered business elsewhere. The court gives him the landing's worth in silver.
Offer him the lots on the altar
Two slips of a twig, one cut with a cross, wrapped in wool on the altar. A boy draws. The cross is yours. Nobody argues with that.
The boy draws the plain slip. You pay, and wonder for a year about the boy.
Offer him the lower half of the landing
He takes it at once, which tells you what his claim was worth. His boat lies next to yours now, and his dog.
The count's man and the tally stick
The count's man comes at Martinmas with the split stick that matches yours. The notches are the same on both halves. He asks, politely, how the year was.
A hall door in November rain: a man in a good cloak and a sword holding up half a notched stick, the merchant holding the other half against it so the notches meet.
Give him a cask for himself, and ask till Easter
He takes the cask as a courtesy and says the count is a patient man in winter. The notches stay as they are till the water opens.
Offer to carry the count's wine in spring for nothing
He writes nothing down, because he cannot write. He holds up four fingers: four casks to the count's hall by midsummer, with no freight. Till then nobody speaks of the debt.
Pour him ale and tell him the truth
He drinks, listens, and counts the notches again with his thumb. He will say what he heard. The day is the day.
The tenth
The priest has reckoned your tithe: a tenth of the year's gain, as the king's law has had it since your father's time. He has reckoned it generously, in the church's favour.
A priest at a small table in a church porch with a tally board, a merchant counting pennies onto it one at a time, a queue of neighbours behind pretending not to count too.
Pay it in full
Thirty pennies on the altar. The priest says your name in the prayers at Christmas, in front of everybody.
Pay it in wax
A cake of good wax for the altar candles. He weighs it in his hands and decides it is a tenth.
Plead a poor year
He looks at your boat, then at your shoes, and lets it stand till next year.
He has seen what you landed in September. He says so, in church.
Boats for the watch
The count's man reads out the summons at the church door: boats and men are wanted to keep watch at the river mouth from Easter, against the Northmen. Your boat is named.
A church door on a grey morning: an armed man reading from a parchment he holds upside down, a clerk whispering the words to him, boatmen listening with folded arms.
Go, with the boat, for forty days
Forty days at the river mouth in the rain, watching for sails that do not come. The count's man marks your name. The trading season starts without you.
Send a man in your place, with his bread
A cousin goes for forty pennies and his food. The count's man accepts him, after looking at his arms.
Stay away
The Northmen do not come this year, and nobody counts the boats.
They count the boats. The fine for a man of your means is five shillings, and the count's man collects it himself.
A stranger at Martinmas

A Northumbrian trader lost his ship on the bar in October and has lived on the priest's bread since. He asks to lodge with you till the sea opens. By law and custom, the host answers for what his guest does.
A lean man in a salt-stained English cloak standing in the rain outside a door, a bundle under his arm, the firelight from inside on his face.
Give him a place at your fire
He is a quiet guest. By Easter you have his speech whole, the names of the men to see at Eoforwic, and his word that your boat will never pay for a berth there.
He is a good guest until he hits the toll man's nephew. You answer for it, as the host must. He is very sorry, in two languages.
Lodge him for his work on the boat
He knows boats. He tars and rivets beside your men all winter and corrects their English.
Leave him with the priest
The priest keeps him. At Easter he takes the first ship west and nods to you from the bank.
The hungry spring
The granaries are low and the new rye is green in the fields. Grain is at three times its harvest price. There are faces at the church door, and you have a store.
A church door in thin spring light, a line of gaunt people with bowls, a priest ladling from a pot; a well-fed man in a merchant's cloak crossing the yard, not looking.
Eat thin till the rye comes
Thin ale and porridge till June. The men are lean and short-tempered and alive.
Give at the church door
A measure a week goes to the priest for the poor, and it is known whose it is.
Sell your store at the price there is
You sell rye at the famine price to those who have silver. They pay. They remember.
You sell at the famine price. The count's man asks what a measure cost you at harvest, takes the difference for the king, and tells the bank why.
The cattle sickness
The cattle sickness has come down the river from the east. Your two oxen, that haul the boat out and pull the neighbour's plough, are down in the byre and will not get up.
A dim byre: two oxen lying in straw with their heads stretched out, a man standing over them with his hand on a post, a boy at the door holding a bucket.
Kill them now and save the hides
Two hides, scraped and salted. The meat is burned, on the priest's advice. In spring the men haul the boat down themselves.
Buy an ox from the upland at the plague price
One thin ox for the price of three. It hauls the boat and looks at you as if it knows.
Wait and pray
One gets up on the ninth day. Nobody can say why. The priest can.
They die in the night. The hides are spoiled by the time you admit it.
Sickness in the town
A mild wet winter, and after it a sickness that goes from house to house along the bank. The priest is burying two a day. Your household is well, so far.
A muddy lane between houses in rain, two men carrying a third on a hurdle toward a small church, shuttered doors on both sides.
Stay, and keep the door shut
You live on what is in the house for a month and see nobody. It passes the door.
It comes in anyway, with the water or the air. Nobody dies. Nobody is strong at Easter.
Take the household up the river to kin
A month on a cousin's farm above the flood line, eating his bacon. When you come back the bank is quieter than it was.
Help carry the sick to the church
You carry and dig for three weeks, and it does not touch you. The priest says that is grace. The oldest of your men says it is luck, and that the two are the same thing.
You carry and dig for three weeks, and then you are carried yourself. You live.
Word from the river mouth

A fisherman from the mouth says the heathen men's ships have been seen off the islands, and that they will come up the river with the first east wind, as they did last year. The count's guard is forty men and a ditch.
A dark room, one rushlight: a man on his knees lifting a hearthstone with an iron bar, a small clay pot beside him; through the half-open door, a river and stars.
Bury the silver under the hearth
At night, alone, a pot under the third hearthstone. Nobody knows but you. Remember to tell someone, or it will lie there till the end of the world.
Carry the household and the chest to Traiectum, behind the wall
The bishop's old Roman wall is not much, but it is a wall. You pay a cousin for a corner of his floor till midsummer.
Stay, and trust the count's guard
You stay. The boat is ready to float at an hour's notice, which is its own kind of trust.
A monk with a book chest
A monk on his way to the bishop is held here by the weather and by a chest of books too heavy for the road. He will teach letters for his bread until the thaw.
A monk in a travel-stained habit sitting on a heavy iron-bound chest in a doorway, sleet behind him, a wax tablet already in his hand.
Lodge him, and sit down to learn
A wax tablet, a stylus and the Lord's Prayer, every evening till Lent. Your hand is bad. You can read the toll man's charter now, which is what you wanted.
Lodge him, and let the boy learn
The boy has the letters in a month and corrects your tallies in two. The monk says he has had worse pupils in the cloister.
Send him on to the priest's house
The priest takes him in. All winter you hear the two of them arguing about the date of Easter.
A Dane for the winter
A Dane who trades whetstones and furs has missed the last fair wind home. He asks for a roof and offers what he has: his speech, his letters, and stories about a king nobody here has heard of.
A fair-haired man by the fire with a whetstone on a thong at his belt, cutting marks into a stick with a small knife, a child leaning on his knee to watch.
Have him teach you his speech
By Candlemas you can bargain, count and insult in it. He says you sound like a man from Jutland with a cold.
Talk with him every night till you have it whole
By Easter you dream in it. He says you now sound like a man from Jutland.
Have him cut the rune row for you
Sixteen staves on a stick of ash, and what each one says. You cut your own name. He reads it out, and it is nearly right.
A blind man at the door

A blind singer is led to your door by a child. He knows the wars of the old kings and the deeds of the men of this coast, and asks a place by the fire till the thaw. The Frisians know such singers: the one Liudger healed of his blindness was named Bernlef.
An old man with white eyes and a small harp under his arm, his hand on the shoulder of a ragged child, standing at a door with frost on the thatch above.
A place by the fire till the thaw
Every evening a king dies well. The men stop going to the ale-wife. When he leaves he gives you a song about a singer who lost his place, and says it is not about him.
One night and a meal
He sings of Finn, and the fight in the Frisians' own hall, and everyone is quiet. In the morning the child leads him on.
Ask him for the song of the lone sailor
He has it from an Englishman, he says, and sings it in a mixture of the two. Hail on the deck, and the gannet's cry where laughter should be. Your steersman goes outside for a while.
Half a boat
Your neighbour has oak seasoning behind his house and no silver to pay a wright. He offers you half of a second boat: you pay for the building, he sails her, and what she makes is split.
Two men standing in snow beside a stack of long oak planks under a lean-to, one with his hand flat on the timber, the other looking at it with his arms folded.
Lay your goods together with his
It is sworn before six witnesses at the church door. The keel is laid at Candlemas. From Easter there are two boats, and you will know where the second one is only when somebody tells you.
Take a quarter share and no more
A quarter of her is yours. He sails her where he likes, and brings you a quarter of what she made, with a story.
Keep to one keel
He finds the silver elsewhere, from a man you do not like.
A bone in silk

A man with a pilgrim's staff and a Roman way of talking unwraps a finger bone from a scrap of silk. A martyr's, he says, from the old burying places outside Rome. The price is an insult to the saint, and he is ashamed to name it.
A lean dark man with a pilgrim's staff and a wallet, holding out on his open palm a small bone lying on a square of red silk; a hearth fire lighting it from below.
Buy it, and take it to the priest
The priest turns it over, smells it, and sends to the bishop. Word comes back before Lent: such bones are coming north by the bishop's own roads. It may be laid under the altar.
The priest turns it over twice. 'A pig,' he says, 'and not an old one.' The man with the staff is two days up the road.
Buy it, and put it in the chest with the amber
It lies in the chest among the amber. You do not ask it for anything, and it does not offer.
Send for the priest to question him
By the time the priest has his shoes on, the man and the bone are on the road to Traiectum.
The lots
The wise woman offers to cast the lots for your spring: which way to sail first. Your grandfather would not have left the bank without it. The priest has preached against it twice this winter.
An old woman kneeling on a floor by firelight with a white cloth spread before her and three short twigs on it, a man standing over her with his arms crossed.
Let her cast
Three slips of a fruit tree on a white cloth. She lifts them one at a time and says: north first, and not before the new moon. The men who keep the old ways are content.
Cast them yourself, at night
You cut the slips as your grandfather did and throw them on your own cloak. They say what you had already decided. That is what they are for.
Send her away, and tell the priest
The priest is pleased. The wise woman is not, and she is the one who is sent for when a child comes.
A vow in the dark of the year
At the worst of the winter, with the roof groaning under the wind, your wife says the house has had more luck than thanks. A vow could be made: a journey when the water opens, or wax for an altar.
A man and a woman by a banked fire at night, the thatch above them bowed by wind, her hand raised as if counting on her fingers.
Vow a journey to Boniface's church at Doccinga
It is said aloud at the hearth, so it counts. Before next winter the boat must lie at Doccinga and alms be given there.
Vow wax to Saint Martin at Traiectum
Two cakes of wax, to be laid on Saint Martin's altar before midsummer. The saint is known to keep accounts.
Vow nothing
You say that God has your tally already. Your wife says that is what worries her.
For the man you lost
One of yours is dead this year. The crew have not spoken of what should be done for him, and are waiting to see whether you will.
A landing in winter dusk: a new oak post with letters cut in it standing at the water's edge, four men round it with their heads bare, a boat hauled up behind.
Thirty masses, and his name in the priest's book
The priest sings the thirtieth mass on a wet Tuesday with all your men standing at the back. His name is written where it will be read.
Cut a marker with his name
An oak post at the head of the landing, with his name cut by your own hand. Boats that pass can read who he was.
Drink his funeral ale and tell what he did
One night, one cask, and every story about him told twice. Some of them are true. It is what he would have asked for.

inheritance.about: WHAT AN HEIR INHERITS (research_indie_and_concept.md 4.4: 'the heir takes the house, the chart's lifted fog, the chest, one feud and one friend'; npc_text_encounters.md 2.5: at a succession every feeling toward the merchant is halved and memories keep their generation). A life ends by age, sickness, wreck or ruin; the house goes on. The engine's 'generation' goes up by one.

who.note: No kinsman can dispute it: there is no lawsuit and no year lost.

who.heir: the eldest child who has come of age
who.note: If he sailed with his father (flag.house_heir_aboard) he keeps the crew's heart as it was; if he kept the house (flag.house_heir_ashore) he keeps the home port's standing whole instead of halved.

who.heir: a child not yet twelve, with the widow holding the house
who.note: The steersman sails the boat on shares until the child is twelve: the house's gain is halved for those years, which pass in one reckoning each.
He takes the house as a son would. The dead man's blood kin are cool for a generation.

who.heir: a brother's or sister's son, or a wife's brother
who.note: The nearest kinsman takes it, with a year lost to the dividing.

who.heir: a sworn partner, who buys the boat from the widow
who.note: The house goes on under his name. Kin ties are lost; the partner's own friends are gained.

The count takes the boat for the debt and the church the rest for the soul. A new man of the same bank begins with one small boat, the count's debt, and the dead man's chart, bought from the priest for the price of a mass.

keeps.rule: every hull the house owns, with what is fitted to it (unlock_upgrade_); a lent ship (a minster's, a bishop's) goes back to its lord
every text, every riddle answered or open, every price note and the merchant's own notes
the fog stays lifted where the house has been, and every unlock_pilot_ flag stays
two thirds of it: see 'pays' for the widow's third and the rest
keeps.source: the Ripuarian Franks' law gave a widow a third of what the pair had gained together (Lex Ribuaria 41) (?)

keeps.rule: all of it, on the same day
keeps.source: DECISIONS.md 10: the debt is a fixed sum due on a day

keeps.rule: commissions taken and vows made (flags vow_...) bind the heir until their day
the person whose feeling toward the dead man was highest keeps it whole
the person whose feeling was lowest keeps it whole, and says so ('your father cheated my father': npc.<role>.generation < generation)
every other feeling toward the house is halved; standing at every port is halved toward nothing, except as rank 2 says
every unlock_kin_, unlock_relic_ and unlock_heirloom_ flag
every unlock_work_ flag: the town remembers who paid
Frisian; the tongue of a foreign wife (flag.house_wife_foreign) or of a foster-son in the house, in full; a tongue the heir sailed two seasons beside, in part
learned.latin at 1 if he was schooled (flag.house_heir_lettered); learned.runes at 0.5 if he was fostered in the north (flag.house_heir_norse) or left the runed knife; otherwise nothing
kept, while the house has a ship of its own, and after the heriot is paid

pays.rule: if a wife lives (flag.house_wed): she keeps her morning-gift and a third, and stays in the house. It is not lost to the house: it is the household's keep and the daughters' portions.
pays.source: Lex Ribuaria 41 (?); in Kent a widow with a living child had half (Æthelberht 78) (?)

pays.what: the soul's gift and the burial
pays.rule: always, where the port is Christian: unlocks_793.json memorial_churchyard. A wrecked man has masses and no grave.
pays.source: soul-scot at the open grave (V Æthelred 12) (?)

only if the dead man had a thegn's right: a horse with its gear and his weapons, or their worth, to the king

pays.d: a fifth of the silver each
pays.rule: sons shared alike among Franks and Frisians: the heir keeps boat and plot and owes each other grown child a share in silver (the engine keeps one child only today: see needs)
pays.source: partible inheritance in the Frankish laws (?)

tongues, letters and runes, except as 'keeps' says

lines: And {heir} his son took to the house.
And {heir}, his sister's son, took to the house, for he had no child.

And there was none to take to the house.

remembered.about: TWELVE WAYS A LIFE IS REMEMBERED. When a merchant of the house dies, the chronicle gets one entry for him: the highest of these whose 'when' holds (12 is the highest). 'when' is in the engine's grammar where it can be; 'also' says in words what the engine cannot yet count. {name}, {home}, {heir}, {port}, {church}, {feast} and {lord} are filled in; the heir's line from inheritance.lines is added after it. The entries are the game's own words in the Chronicle's manner, not quotations.
remembered.voice: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's flat voice: 'This year died ...', where he lies, who took to his place; no praise beyond one plain clause. Models read for the shape (not quoted): the annal for 793 (texts_793.json chronicle_793, Giles 1847); the annal for 897, which names 'Wulfheard the Frisian, Æbbe the Frisian and Æthelhere the Frisian' among the dead of Alfred's ships (?); the annal for 901 on Alfred's death and the length of his reign (?); the obits that end 'and his body rests at' a named church (?).

lives.name: The beggar
lives.also: no boat, no plot and no heir at the death

lives.name: The drowned man
lives.also: died in a wreck, with no heir aboard or ashore
lives.entry: This year {name} of {home} was lost at sea with his boat and all his men, about {feast}. Nothing came ashore.

lives.name: The man who fled
lives.also: died away from home after the deed fled_kings_men or taken_for_judgement
lives.entry: This year {name} the merchant died out of the land. He had fled the king's men and was not seen again at {home}; and no one set up a marker.

lives.name: The hard man
lives.when: silver >= 600 and (flag.house_hard_name or flag.perjured or flag.unlock_relic_false_bone)
lives.entry: This year died {name} of {home}. He left silver. It was said that he kept what was owed to dead men's widows, and few went to the grave.

lives.name: The hired hand
lives.also: the house had no boat of its own at the death
lives.entry: This year died {name}, who once had a boat of his own and afterwards pulled an oar in other men's. He was a good seaman.

lives.name: The small trader
lives.entry: This year died {name} the merchant, in his bed at {home}. He had one boat and owed nothing.

lives.name: The good neighbour
lives.also: the deed gave_alms done in at least three winters
lives.entry: This year died {name} of {home}, a merchant. He gave bread at the church door in the hungry years, and the whole bank followed him to the grave.

lives.when: debt = 0 and (flag.unlock_partner_neighbour or flag.unlock_partner_kinsman or flag.unlock_partner_felagi or flag.unlock_partner_widow)
lives.also: three keels or more on the water, or two factors
lives.entry: This year died {name}, who had three keels on the water and men of his own at {port}. The ships sailed at Easter as before.

lives.name: The far-farer
lives.when: debt = 0 and (flag.unlock_pilot_volkhov or flag.unlock_pilot_malaren or flag.unlock_pilot_estmere) and (flag.unlock_pilot_humber or flag.unlock_pilot_thames or flag.unlock_pilot_loire)
lives.also: called at thirty ports or more in his life
lives.entry: This year died {name}, whom men called the far-farer. He had seen the lake of the Svear and the river of the Rus, and had crossed the wide sea more times than he had fingers. His sounding lead hangs in the church at {home}.

lives.name: The friend of God's poor
lives.when: debt = 0 and (flag.unlock_work_dorestad_hospice or flag.unlock_work_sliesthorp_bell or flag.unlock_work_birka_church or flag.unlock_work_ripa_church or flag.relic_given)
lives.also: a memorial of kind book of life, or two works
lives.entry: This year died {name} the merchant, a friend of God's poor. He gave the bell at {port} and the bread at {home}, and his name is in the book. His body rests at {church}.

lives.name: The man of rank
lives.when: flag.unlock_title_thegn or flag.unlock_title_tiel_brother or flag.unlock_title_palace_merchant or flag.unlock_title_frisian_guild or flag.unlock_title_moneyer
lives.entry: This year died {name}, a merchant who had so thriven that he was worthy of a thegn's right; for he had crossed the wide sea three times at his own cost. His body rests at {church}.

variants.unlock_title_tiel_brother: This year died {name}, one of the merchants of Tiel, who swear and drink together. His brothers bore him to the grave and paid for it from the common purse.
variants.unlock_title_palace_merchant: This year died {name}, the emperor's merchant, who went each May to the palace. The letter he held went back to the chamber.
variants.unlock_title_frisian_guild: This year died {name}. The Frisians' guild-brothers had a stone raised after him. God help his soul.
variants.unlock_title_moneyer: This year died {name} the moneyer, whose name is on the king's pennies. Both his hands were on him when he was buried.

lives.name: The king's friend
lives.entry: This year, {feast}, died {name} the merchant, the king's friend, who sat in his hall and told him of seas he had not seen. He was a Frisian by birth. {lord} sent a cloak for the bier.

needs: The winter screen itself: it sets 'flag wintering for <days>' and draws the cards as 'how_it_runs' says. Until it exists the cards never come (every 'when' asks for flag.wintering); with the flag set by hand they come as ordinary harbour cards in the long-stay draw, in their months.

A line shown after a choice: the writing keys '<label_key>.after', and '.after.success' and '.after.failure' for a chance, hold each outcome as a fact. The panel shows only the effects' own words today.
A picture key for each card: 'art.<card id>' is in the writing block, as BRIEF_2.md asks.
Numbers the reckoning needs and the engine does not keep: the year's gain or loss after wages and bread, boats lost, men dead, ports first seen, sea crossings in a ship of one's own.
An effect to pay part of the debt ('debt -n') and one to put the debt's day off ('debt_due +days'): harbour.winter.count_debt can only set flag debt_grace.
A deed for helping neighbours (fire, flood, sickness): the cards use gave_alms, the nearest there is.
The house keeps one child (flags house_child, house_child_small). More children, daughters' portions and brothers' shares need a list of kin with ages.
A vow not kept in its 300 days should cost the crew's heart, and a promise broken (promised_river_boy) the bank's standing: cards at sea and in spring should read the flags.
A quarter share (flag house_share_quarter), a factor's keep, a charter's render and a guild's purse are all paid or received at the reckoning: the screen should run them.
A port at home: there is no variable for the house's home port, so the flood card lists the low ports by id and the others trust flag.wintering.
Forcing a card in the chronicle's own year (the flood of 838, the cattle plague of 809 to 810, the pestilence of 801 and 808, the famine years): the notes say which.
